# Sacubitril/Valsartan (Angiotensin Receptor–Neprilysin Inhibition) in Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction and rationale

Heart failure (HF) remains a leading cause of hospitalisation and mortality worldwide, and for decades inhibition of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS) with angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors formed the cornerstone of therapy for HF with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) [1]. Sacubitril/valsartan, formerly designated LCZ696, represents a complementary pharmacological strategy. It is a combination of a neprilysin inhibitor and an angiotensin II type 1 receptor blocker; oral administration delivers valsartan and the sacubitril prodrug, which is metabolised to the active metabolite sacubitrilat, inhibiting degradation of natriuretic peptides and enhancing their biological activity [2]. Inhibition of neprilysin increases levels of natriuretic peptides, bradykinin, and adrenomedullin, thus resulting in natriuresis and vasodilatation [3], while the valsartan component simultaneously blocks the deleterious effects of angiotensin II. The molecule was deliberately designed to avoid the excess angioedema risk seen when neprilysin and ACE are inhibited together [4].

## Pivotal evidence in HFrEF: PARADIGM-HF

The landmark PARADIGM-HF trial established the clinical value of this approach. Investigators compared LCZ696 with enalapril in patients who had heart failure with a reduced ejection fraction, in whom enalapril had previously been shown to improve survival [4]. Titrated to a target dose of 200 mg twice daily, sacubitril/valsartan significantly reduced the primary composite endpoint of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalisation by 20% compared with enalapril [4]. The trial was stopped early when it demonstrated overwhelming benefit [5]. This benefit was driven by reductions in both modes of cardiovascular death: most deaths were cardiovascular, with sudden death the most common cause followed by worsening HF, and the reduction in mortality was similar for sudden death and pump failure (20% and 21% relative risk reduction, respectively) [6]. The hazard ratio for the primary endpoint was 0.80, and benefit was consistent regardless of background pharmacological and device therapy [7]. Sacubitril/valsartan also reduced both first and recurrent HF hospitalisations [8] and slowed clinical progression in survivors [9].

## Mechanisms: reverse remodelling and biomarkers

The mechanistic basis of benefit has been explored in dedicated studies. In the open-label PROVE-HF study, reduction in NT-proBNP concentration was weakly yet significantly correlated with improvements in markers of cardiac volume and function at 12 months, suggesting reverse cardiac remodelling [10]. By contrast, in the EVALUATE-HF trial, treatment with sacubitril-valsartan compared with enalapril did not significantly reduce central aortic stiffness, indicating that clinical benefit is unrelated to changes in pulsatile arterial load [11]. Together these findings support remodelling and wall-stress reduction rather than arterial mechanics as principal mediators.

## Safety and tolerability

A consistent safety signal across trials has been reassuring. Among patients taking a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, severe hyperkalaemia was more common with enalapril than with sacubitril/valsartan, potentially improving tolerability of comprehensive therapy [12]. In the acute setting, rates of renal dysfunction, hyperkalaemia, and symptomatic hypotension did not differ significantly between groups, and there was only one case of angioedema [13].

## Extending to acute and de novo heart failure

Because PARADIGM-HF enrolled stable ambulatory outpatients, the PIONEER-HF and TRANSITION trials examined initiation in hospitalised patients. PIONEER-HF was a randomised, double-blind trial of in-hospital initiation of sacubitril/valsartan versus enalapril in patients stabilised during hospitalisation for acute decompensated HF, in whom sacubitril/valsartan decreased the risk of cardiovascular outcomes [14]; the clinical benefit was driven by reduced rehospitalisation [15]. The TRANSITION study showed that initiation early after haemodynamic stabilisation was feasible, with a protocol reflecting daily clinical practice and label-based dosing [16].

## Preserved and mildly reduced ejection fraction

In HF with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), the phase 2 PARAMOUNT trial provided proof of concept: LCZ696 reduced NT-proBNP to a greater extent than valsartan at 12 weeks and was well tolerated [17]. The definitive PARAGON-HF trial, however, did not show a significantly lower composite of total HF hospitalisations and cardiovascular death compared with valsartan alone, though there was modest improvement in NYHA class and less renal function decline [18]. A pre-specified pooled analysis with PARAGLIDE-HF later supported benefit in patients with mildly reduced or preserved ejection fraction, particularly nearer the lower ejection-fraction range [19]. Renal outcomes also favoured the ARNI in this population [20].

## Acute myocardial infarction

The PARADISE-MI trial tested whether benefit extended to high-risk myocardial infarction. Sacubitril–valsartan was not associated with a significantly lower incidence of death from cardiovascular causes or incident heart failure than ramipril among patients with acute myocardial infarction [21], although echocardiographic substudies suggested favourable effects on remodelling [22], and a focused study found neprilysin inhibition modestly affected remodelling late after infarction [23].

## Guideline status and conclusions

These data have reshaped guidelines. The 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA guideline and the 2021 ESC guideline both incorporate ARNI as a foundational therapy for HFrEF, with the ARNI recommended in preference to an ACE inhibitor in suitable patients [24][25], reflecting a Class I status as a replacement for an ACE inhibitor [26]. Contemporary practical reviews emphasise a continuum of use across the patient journey [27], including functional mitral regurgitation [28] and mode-of-death considerations relevant to defibrillator decisions [29]. Meta-analyses confirm consistent reductions in mortality and HF events relative to RAAS inhibitor comparators [30]. In summary, sacubitril/valsartan is firmly established as a disease-modifying therapy in HFrEF, with a more nuanced role in milder phenotypes of preserved ejection fraction and limited evidence post-infarction.
